claim: Modernity has traditionally been presented as the age when artifacts supplant nature and destroy the originally given natural environment through a process of de-naturalization, but Hannah Arendt questioned this conviction.
supporting_excerpt: Modernity, in philosophical and sociological literature, has “traditionally” been presented as the age when artifacts supplant nature and destroy the originally given natural environment. The process of modernization, from this point of view, is the process of de-naturalization . This widely shared conviction has ba - sically been questioned by Hannah Arendt.

claim: Arendt's political ontology in The Human Condition is based on a phenomenological approach rooted in German Existenz-philosophy.
supporting_excerpt: The political ontology explained in the book was based on a phenomenological approach rooted in the German Existenz -philosophy.

claim: The search for an extraterrestrial Archimedean point involves a radical modification of the human condition.
supporting_excerpt:
The search for an ex -

human condition so far having been determined by the circumstances of our native

claim: Labor is described as a mere animal activity in Arendt's ontology, wherein humanity is considered the most dangerous of animal races.
supporting_excerpt: Labor , summarizing this train of thought, is a mere animal activity in the ontology of Arendt.

claim: Action is identified as the highest and most specifically human activity, taking place in the world of things created by homo faber.
supporting_excerpt: The third and highest stage of human existence, in the ontology of Arendt, is the level of action taking place in the world of things created by homo faber . Action is the most specifically human activity; to act and to be free is the same, Arendt concludes.

claim: Process is the antithesis of action, functioning as a sequence of changes predetermined by an inner impersonal law that creates a terrain of necessity.
supporting_excerpt: Process is the antithesis of action which needs free, undetermined human individuals being able to initiate new beginnings in the world. Process is the sequence of changes predetermined by an inner impersonal law regulating the order of these changes. The ensuing events of a process are links in a cause–effect chain where the later states of temporal development are casually determined by the former ones. The realm of processes is a terrain of necessity.

claim: Modernity in its first phase is characterized by the victory of homo faber using means-end rationality to produce artificial things, with fabrication inherently entailing violence against nature.
supporting_excerpt: Modernity, at least in its first phase, for her, means the victory of homo faber who, under the guidance of means-end rationality , began, in ever-increasing amount and speed, to produce large variety of artificial things. Homo faber seemed to become the master of the Earth who continuously expands the reach of his power over his environment. The activity of fabrication inherently entails the element of violence directed against lifeless and living nature.

claim: Fabrication inevitably involves an over-all reification of nature and acts as a destroyer of nature through an element of violation and violence.
supporting_excerpt: This element of violation and violence is present in all fabrication and homo faber , the creator of human artifice, has always been a destroyer of nature.

claim: In the second phase of modernity, animal laborans rises to dominance and technological productivity paradoxically annihilates the lasting artificial world by flooding it with natural processes.
supporting_excerpt: The second phase of modernity entails the victorious rise of animal laborans who embodies the natural part of human being ensuring the futile, perishable goods of consumption needed for the mere biological survival of humanity as one among other animal spe - cies. The thing-character of the artificial world created by the irresistibly expanding technology is melting away in an ever growing speed. Natural processes are flooding the lasting artificial constructions of human existence.

claim: Arendt asserts that the rationality required for constructing machines and launching artificial processes is an animal rather than a human ability, functioning as a modified animal instinct to maintain biological existence.
supporting_excerpt:
Arendt puts forward an astonishing and strange assertion: rationality needed for construction of machines and getting involved in launching artificial processes, an sich , for her, is an animal and not human ability. Rationality, in her argumentation, a special modified kind of animal instinct, whose function is to find the necessary means to reach the shared end of all living organ -
isms; the maintenance of their biological existence

claim: Modern technology does not build a lasting artificial human world, but instead serves to fulfill consumption needs and ensure the continuous functioning of human metabolism with nature.
supporting_excerpt:
The emerging gigantic machine of human technology does not contribute to the upkeep of the lasting artificial human world; it serves to fulfill the needs of consumption, in other words, it ensures, in an ever-expanding cycles, the un -
disturbed functioning of the processes of human metabolism with nature.

claim: In her closing chapter, Arendt returns to the narrative of cultural criticism where re-naturalization and the fading out of action embody the main threat of modernity rather than environmental pollution.
supporting_excerpt: It is re-naturalization, for her, and not human construed artifice which embodies the main threat of modernity. She more fears for the fading out of action from the world than the pollution of the environment.
